clue.text: I follow wild crocuses after start of spring

indicators.note: after places the rearranged flowers behind the opening letter
the start of the word spring gives just its opening letter
wild suggests the letters of crocuses run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone describes themselves trailing a patch of untamed spring crocuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I follow' reads as part of a sentence but is the definition: the speaker is one who comes after. 'wild' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: One who comes next in line or takes over a role is the one who follows, so the speaker names themself.

clue.text: To the north, British India's leader owns local address

indicators.note: in a down entry, going to the north means reading upwards, so the pieces are turned round
the leader of India's is its first letter

parts.note: owns means has

explanation.surface: A geography note about a British leader in India and how he is addressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To the north' reverses BIHAS, built from B, I and HAS, giving the word read upwards. Sahib was a respectful form of address in colonial India.
explanation.definitionFit: Sahib is the term of address for a gentleman or master used in India, hence a local address.

clue.text: Forged bar: it contains iron

parts.note: a bar in a pub or shop is a counter
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
taken as written

explanation.surface: A forged iron bar, with 'it contains iron' as an explanation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forged' could mean shaped by a smith, fitting the iron bar, but here it means faked. 'contains' marks the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forged is a fake copy, which is exactly what a counterfeit item is.

clue.text: Some in Jobcentre attacked request

indicators.note: Some in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A news report of an attack on a Jobcentre, a UK state employment office.
explanation.definitionFit: To entreat someone is to beg or ask earnestly, a formal synonym of request as a verb.

clue.text: Glaswegian, maybe without charge and unpunished

parts.note: a Glaswegian is one example of a Scot, a native of Scotland
something without charge costs nothing, is free

explanation.surface: Someone from Glasgow is let off without being charged and escapes punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, so a Glaswegian is a Scot; 'maybe' marks the example.
explanation.definitionFit: To get off scot-free is an idiom for escaping without any penalty at all.

clue.text: Problem in flash photo initially exposed in colour again

indicators.note: the second in puts the opening letter inside the dyeing word

parts.note: to colour something again is to redye it

indicators.note: initially means take just the opening letter of exposed

explanation.surface: Photography advice: a problem in a flash shot, an overexposed image coloured again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places E, from 'initially exposed', inside REDYE.
explanation.definitionFit: Red-eye is the red glow in subjects' pupils caused by a camera flash reflecting off the retina.

clue.text: Knock back wines to get wobbly

indicators.note: knock back here means turn back, so the wines are read in reverse order

parts.note: ports are fortified wines from Portugal

explanation.surface: Drinking down wines until you are unsteady on your feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock back' looks like drinking, but it reverses PORTS. In British slang, 'throw a wobbly' means have a tantrum, and a strop is the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A strop is British slang for a sulky fit of temper, the same noun sense as a wobbly.

clue.text: Pixie lovers flipped a bit

indicators.note: flipped says the whole phrase is turned over and read backwards

parts.note: a pixie is a kind of elf
fans are lovers or devotees of something

explanation.surface: Fans of pixies went crazy just a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipped' reverses ELFFANS as one string. 'flipped a bit' reads as 'went slightly mad'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snaffle is a simple jointed mouthpiece for a horse, one type of bit.

clue.text: Speed reduced in desert …

indicators.note: reduced says the word for speed is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: speed is rate, as in rate of travel

explanation.surface: Speed limits lowered in a desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' looks like a place, but it is the verb: to rat on someone is to desert them.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to abandon or betray one's side, a verb sense matching desert.

clue.text: … that one in photo, almost completely lawless

indicators.note: in places the pair of pieces inside the word for a photo

parts.note: pic is short for picture, a photo
the ellipsis carries on from the previous clue, so that means its answer, the rodent
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: almost says the word for completely loses its final letter

parts.note: completely means all

explanation.surface: Continuing a story: a desert creature caught on camera, behaving almost entirely outside the law.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses carry on from 7 Down, so 'that' points to its answer. 'in' marks the container and 'almost' the shortening.
explanation.definitionFit: Piratical means like a pirate, someone operating outside the law, so lawless.

clue.text: Frequent answer in search

indicators.note: in puts the single letter inside the word for a search

parts.note: a hunt is a search

explanation.surface: A common answer turns up in a search.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frequent' is the verb, to visit often, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To haunt a place is to visit it habitually, the verb sense of frequent.

clue.text: Art's model, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: here the apostrophe is ignored and its letters are used in full

explanation.surface: Describing a person who sits as a model for art.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'possibly' rearranges ARTS and MODEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A great painting by a classic European painter is something art students copy as a model of excellence.

clue.text: Escalation of a small flap to an international storm?

definitions.text: Escalation of a small flap to an international storm?

parts.words: Escalation of a small flap to an international storm?
parts.note: chaos theory says a tiny wing beat could eventually set off a distant storm

explanation.surface: A minor political fuss grows into a global crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flap' reads as a minor fuss but literally means the beat of an insect's wing.
explanation.definitionFit: The chaos-theory idea that tiny causes can have huge consequences, illustrated by a wing beat starting a far-off storm.

clue.text: Legal handover's usual procedure no longer followed?

parts.note: ex means former, describing something no longer in force
a tradition is the customary, usual way of doing things

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the usual legal process for handing people over has been abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as EX-TRADITION, a custom no longer kept; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Extradition is the formal surrender of a suspect by one state to another for trial.

clue.text: Special hotelier with the Queen's drink

parts.note: César Ritz was the Swiss hotelier who founded the Ritz hotels
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: A special hotel owner shares a drink with the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A spritzer is a long drink of white wine mixed with soda water.

clue.text: Drawn into dumps for retirement years?

indicators.note: into puts the word for drawn inside the word for dumps

parts.note: sties are pigsties, filthy dumps
a drawn game is even, level

explanation.surface: Being dragged into the doldrums once you stop working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn' looks like a verb but means level, as in a drawn match. The question mark marks retirement years as only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: People in their seventies are typically retired, so the decade loosely serves as retirement years.

clue.text: Frantic spasm after brief cry of frustration

indicators.note: after puts the spasm behind the shortened cry
brief says the exclamation is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: heck is a mild exclamation of annoyance
a tic is an involuntary muscle spasm

explanation.surface: A frantic twitch following a short outburst of annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brief' trims HECK to HEC.
explanation.definitionFit: Hectic means full of frenzied activity, the same as frantic.

clue.text: After training, a student understood

indicators.note: training reshapes the letters of a student into a new form

explanation.surface: A student finally gets it after some coaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'understood' is the sense of implied, not grasped. 'After training' rearranges A STUDENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left unspoken but implied is understood, the sense of an understood condition.

clue.text: Audience member having a jug after six

indicators.note: after places the jug behind the numeral

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
a ewer is a large water jug

explanation.surface: Someone in the audience holding a jug at six o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A viewer watches a show, so one is part of a television or theatre audience.

clue.text: I've refined taste before engaging self-righteous copper

indicators.note: engaging means holding within, so the word for before encloses the other pieces

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
pi is British informal for pious, sanctimonious
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Someone with refined palate boasts before involving a smug police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' suggests a policeman but is the metal. 'engaging' puts PICU inside ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicure is a connoisseur of fine food and drink, someone whose palate is refined.

clue.text: Cold shower startling all of NSW

indicators.note: startling suggests the letters are jolted out of their places into a new order

explanation.surface: A freak bout of frigid weather surprising all of New South Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: NSW is New South Wales, an Australian state, where such weather would surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow is literally a cold precipitation, a shower of frozen flakes.

clue.text: Meanders over evacuated town near Eton

parts.note: a road that meanders winds

indicators.note: evacuated means emptied, keeping only the outside letters of over

explanation.surface: A river meanders past a cleared-out town near the famous school.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the English public school beside the Thames; WINDSOR, with its royal castle, lies across the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Windsor is the Berkshire town facing Eton across the River Thames.

clue.text: Dodge unknown end of ride after yell from roller coaster?

indicators.note: after puts the unknown and the last letter behind the yell

parts.note: whee is a cry of thrilled delight on a fairground ride
z is a mathematical unknown, like x and y

indicators.note: the end of ride is its last letter

explanation.surface: A funfair scene: someone dodges the ending of a scary ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodge' is the noun, a crafty trick; WHEEZE is British slang for a clever scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheeze is British informal for a clever scheme or trick, the same as a dodge.

clue.text: Regardless of having no social position

parts.note: no means not
with means having, as in a house with a garden
standing is status or social position

explanation.surface: Someone indifferent to people who lack any rank in society.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a whole phrase, but the answer splits into three ordinary words that together mean lacking status.
explanation.definitionFit: This preposition means in spite of, a formal match for regardless of.

clue.text: More than half of superb Cheddar, say

indicators.note: more than half keeps five of the eight letters of the word for superb, dropping the tail

parts.note: gorgeous means superb or stunning

explanation.surface: Praising a cheese as more than half superb.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar looks like the cheese, but Cheddar Gorge is a ravine in Somerset, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheddar Gorge is a well-known limestone ravine in England, an example of a steep valley.

clue.text: Reckless troublemaker, game to impress?

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous troublemaker
RU is rugby union, a ball game
to dent is to impress, to make a mark in a surface

explanation.surface: A rash troublemaker wondering whether a game will win admiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'impress' looks like 'win admiration' but means press in, making a dent.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprudent means unwise or rash, acting without care, hence reckless.

clue.text: 22 seen regularly in spring

definitions.note: the cross-reference is to 22 Down, read here as a verb meaning overeat

indicators.note: regularly picks every second letter of spring

explanation.surface: Something from another clue turns up every so often in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: Every other letter of sPrInG gives the answer. 22 Down is read as the verb: to stuff yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: To pig out and to stuff oneself both mean eat greedily, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Sportsman's captain, repeatedly losing player's lead

indicators.note: losing says letters are taken out of the word for captain

parts.note: a skipper is a captain of a ship or team

indicators.note: repeatedly means the lead letter is removed twice
the lead of player's is its first letter

explanation.surface: A team captain keeps losing his star player.
explanation.walkthrough: SKIPPER loses P twice, both from 'player's lead', leaving SKIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A skier is someone who competes on skis, a sportsman in that discipline.

clue.text: Play on visit around middle of August

indicators.note: around says the word for visit surrounds the central pair of letters

parts.note: to see a doctor is to visit one

indicators.note: the middle of August is its central two letters

explanation.surface: A summer performance continues on a visit in mid-August.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play on' looks like a pun or a joke, but in music a segue means carrying straight on into the next piece. 'around' marks the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A segue is a smooth transition, in music meaning carry on without a break, like play on.

clue.text: Stoicism, a creed nun revived

indicators.note: revived suggests the letters of the phrase are brought back to life in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A nun's faith is revived through patient fortitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoicism is patient tolerance of hardship, which is what endurance means.
